privacy.shortText: Remote AI models send your photos and descriptions to third-party cloud providers.
privacy.fullText:
When you configure remote AI models (OpenAI, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, Groq, etc.), your photos and the metadata generated by this app may be sent to those providers' servers and processed under their privacy policies. They may store or use this data according to their terms of service.

To keep your data private:
• Local models — run entirely on your device; no data leaves your computer.
• Self-hosted models — Ollama or vLLM on a server you control.
• Enterprise providers — those offering explicit data-retention guarantees.

If you are unsure, selecting all local models is the safest choice.

getting-started.title: Getting Started
getting-started.intro: Welcome to PhotoRAG — an AI-powered photo management system.
getting-started.body:
PhotoRAG helps you organise, describe, and search your entire photo library using local and remote AI models.

During first launch, the Setup Wizard guides you through installing Python dependencies, initialising the database, and choosing which AI models to use (local or remote via API key).

Once setup is complete, the main application opens automatically. You can add photo folders from the Folders page and start processing with the Processing page.
getting-started.examples: Example: install PhotoRAG, run the Setup Wizard, add your 'Vacation 2024' folder in Folders, then go to Processing and click 'Run' — PhotoRAG will automatically generate English descriptions, extract any text visible in photos, and index everything for search.

gallery.title: Gallery
gallery.intro: The Gallery is the main view of your photo library.
gallery.body:
All processed photos appear as cards in the Gallery grid. Each card shows a thumbnail, the auto-generated description, and any tags or categories assigned.

You can sort photos by date, filter by folder or processing status, and click any card to open the Photo Detail page.

Photos that have not yet been processed show a pending indicator.
gallery.examples: Example: open the Gallery and use the filter panel to select tags such as 'sunset' or 'beach', categories such as 'Landscape', a location, and a date range. You can select multiple tags and categories at the same time — each additional selection narrows the results further. Click any card to see the full description and linked documents.

search.title: Search
search.intro: Find photos using natural language or keyword queries.
search.body:
PhotoRAG uses vector embeddings to enable semantic search: you describe what you are looking for in plain language and the system returns the most visually and conceptually similar photos, even if your exact words do not appear in any description.

Keyword search matches exact words in descriptions, tags, and extracted text. You can combine semantic and keyword modes.

Results are ranked by similarity score. Click any result to open the Photo Detail page.
search.examples: Example: type 'dog running on a beach at sunset' — PhotoRAG returns photos matching that scene even if no description contains all those words exactly. Or type 'birthday' to find all photos where birthday-related text was detected or described.

photo-detail.title: Photo Detail
photo-detail.intro: View the full information for a single photo.
photo-detail.body:
The Photo Detail page shows the original image alongside its AI-generated description, assigned tags, categories, and any documents (extracted text) linked to the photo.

You can navigate to the next or previous photo in the current view and open the Photo Edit page to modify metadata.

If translation is enabled and your language is not English, descriptions are shown in your selected language.
photo-detail.examples: Example: click a photo in the Gallery, see its English description alongside the Russian translation (if you set Russian in Settings), and view any text extracted from a receipt or document visible in the photo.

photo-edit.title: Photo Edit
photo-edit.intro: Manually edit a photo's title, description, and tags.
photo-edit.body:
On the Photo Edit page you can override the AI-generated description with your own text, add or remove tags, and change the category.

After saving, the photo is re-indexed so it immediately appears in updated search results. You can also trigger a re-run of AI analysis to regenerate the description from scratch using the current prompt template.
photo-edit.examples: Example: the AI described a photo as 'a group of people indoors' but you know it is your team at a product launch. Edit the description to 'Team at the 2024 product launch, office, evening', add tags 'team work launch', and save.

documents.title: Documents
documents.intro: Browse text documents extracted from your photos.
documents.body:
When photos contain visible text (receipts, invoices, signs, whiteboards, book pages), PhotoRAG uses OCR to extract that text and stores it as a Document linked to the photo.

The Documents page lists all extracted documents. You can search document content, view which photo a document belongs to, and filter by document type.

Documents are also included in semantic search results.
documents.examples: Example: photograph a whiteboard from a meeting. PhotoRAG extracts the text into a Document. Later, search for 'Q3 roadmap' — the meeting whiteboard photo appears in results because its extracted document contains that phrase.

duplicates.title: Duplicates
duplicates.intro: Find and resolve duplicate photos in your library.
duplicates.body:
PhotoRAG detects duplicate photos using a combination of perceptual hashing (for exact or near-exact copies) and semantic similarity (for visually similar but not identical shots).

The Duplicates page groups photos into duplicate clusters. For each cluster you can choose which copy to keep and mark the rest for deletion or archiving. Archiving moves photos to long-term storage without permanently removing them, while deletion moves them to the Garbage page for final review.

You can also keep all copies if all of them are unique in some way.
duplicates.examples: Example: you copied a folder of photos twice by mistake. Open Duplicates — PhotoRAG groups all 200 pairs. Select 'Keep latest' for each group and click 'Remove duplicates' to clean up without losing any unique photos.

garbage.title: Garbage / Bad Photos
garbage.intro: Review and remove low-quality or unwanted photos.
garbage.body:
PhotoRAG automatically detects and flags low-quality photos — blurry shots, overexposed or underexposed images, accidental captures, and photos the AI model rates as uninformative.

Flagged photos appear on the Garbage page. You review each one and choose to restore it to the Gallery, archive it (moves the photo to long-term storage, keeping it accessible but out of the main library), or permanently delete it.

Photos sent to Garbage from the Duplicates page also appear here.
garbage.examples: Example: after importing 1 000 holiday photos, 47 are flagged as blurry or accidental. Open Garbage, review the thumbnails, restore the 5 that are actually fine, and permanently delete the remaining 42 with one click.

chat.title: Chat (Agent AI)
chat.intro: Ask questions about your photo library in natural language.
chat.body:
The Chat page provides a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) interface powered by the configured language model. You type a question or instruction, PhotoRAG searches your photo library for relevant context, and the AI responds using that context.

The AI Agent has access to the following tools:

Search tools: full-text search across descriptions, tags, and extracted documents; semantic (vector) similarity search; search by date range, location, tag, or category; combined multi-filter search.

Photo editing tools: update a photo's description, title, tags, or category; re-run AI analysis on a specific photo.

Photo management tools: delete a photo (moves it to Garbage); archive a photo (moves it to long-term storage); restore a photo from Garbage or archive.

Data extraction tools: extract text from a photo using OCR; retrieve all documents linked to a photo; summarise the contents of a group of photos.

Rating and description tools: assign a quality score to a photo; generate or regenerate the AI description using the active prompt template; translate a description into the configured language.

Undo tool: if the Agent performs an action you did not intend, you can ask it to undo the last action. The Agent will reverse the most recent change it made (for example, restore a deleted photo or revert an edited description).

System prompts for the Agent are configured separately on the Prompts & Templates page. There you can define how the Agent introduces itself, what its default behaviour is, and what constraints apply to its responses.
chat.examples: Example: ask 'What did our team look like in 2023?' — the AI retrieves team photos from 2023, summarises who is in them, and describes the settings. Then ask 'Which of those were taken outdoors?' for a refined answer.

processing.title: Processing
processing.intro: Manage the AI pipeline that analyses your photos.
processing.body:
The Processing page shows a live view of the photo analysis pipeline. It is a read-only monitor: you cannot start, pause, or stop processing from here. Processing is triggered automatically by folder watchers when new photos arrive, or by a manual folder scan started from the Folders page.

Each photo passes through multiple pipeline phases: description generation, translation (if a non-English language is configured), OCR text extraction, duplicate detection, and quality scoring. The page shows each phase as a separate row so you can see exactly which phase each job is in.

For every task you can see how long it has been running, its current status, and — for failed jobs — the full error message. This makes it straightforward to identify which photos failed and why, so you can investigate the root cause before re-triggering a scan.
processing.examples: Example: you notice three jobs have been in the 'description' phase for an unusually long time. Click the task row to see the error: the remote model API returned a timeout. Fix the API connectivity issue, then return to the Folders page and run the scanner again — only the failed photos will be re-queued.

folders.title: Folders
folders.intro: Configure which photo folders PhotoRAG monitors.
folders.body:
PhotoRAG supports two distinct methods for adding photos to your library.

Method 1 — Watcher: you configure a source folder for the Watcher to monitor and a separate storage folder where PhotoRAG will automatically move incoming photos, organising them into subfolders by year, month, and day (the folder structure is fixed in the current version). The Watcher continuously observes the source folder and empties it each time new files appear. This is ideal for automatic phone-sync workflows: for example, configure [Syncthing](https://syncthing.net/) to sync a specific folder from your smartphone to your PC, then point a PhotoRAG Watcher at that sync folder. Photos transfer from your phone to the PC and are immediately ingested, described, and moved into the organised storage folder — freeing up space on the phone automatically.

Method 2 — Scanner: you point the Scanner at an existing folder (for example your home directory or an external drive) and PhotoRAG performs a one-time recursive scan, finding and indexing all image files it discovers. Photos stay in place; they are not moved. The Scanner does not watch for future changes: if you add, move, or delete photos inside the scanned folder afterwards, PhotoRAG is unaware until you run the Scanner again.

Key difference: the Watcher is always on and automatically moves photos into structured storage, making it ideal for ongoing ingestion. The Scanner is a one-shot operation suited to importing an existing photo collection.
folders.examples:
Watcher example: install Syncthing on your phone and PC. Create a sync folder called 'Phone inbox'. Add a PhotoRAG Watcher pointing at 'Phone inbox' as the source and '/Photos/Library' as storage. When you transfer a photo to the sync folder on your phone it arrives on the PC, PhotoRAG picks it up within seconds, describes it, and files it under '/Photos/Library/2025/05/26'. The sync folder is emptied automatically.

Scanner example: you have 5 000 family photos in '/Users/me/Pictures'. Add that path as a Scanner folder. PhotoRAG scans every subfolder, finds all images, and queues them for processing. Run the Scanner again any time you copy new photos into that tree manually.

models.title: Models
models.intro: Configure the AI models used for description, translation, and search.
models.body:
PhotoRAG uses separate models for different tasks: a vision model for generating photo descriptions, a language model for chat and re-writing, a translation model for multilingual support, and an embedding model for semantic search.

Each model can run locally (downloaded to your machine) or remotely via an API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others).

The Models page lets you switch between local and remote mode, enter API keys, and check model download and readiness status.

Data privacy: when you use a local model, all photo data — images, descriptions, extracted text, and search queries — stays entirely on your machine and is never sent to any external server. When you use a remote model, the photo image or its description is sent to the chosen API provider (for example OpenAI) for processing. This means your photos or their content may be stored or logged by that provider according to their own privacy policy. If privacy is a concern, use local models only, or review the privacy policy of your chosen provider before enabling remote mode.
models.examples: Example: switch the vision model from local LLaVA to remote GPT-4o by selecting 'Remote' mode, entering your OpenAI API key, and clicking Save. New photo descriptions will now be generated by GPT-4o without downloading anything locally.

prompts.title: Prompts & Templates
prompts.intro: Customise the instructions given to the AI when describing photos.
prompts.body:
Prompt templates control what the AI writes in photo descriptions. You can create templates for different categories of photos (portraits, landscapes, documents, receipts) and assign them as the default for a folder or globally.

Templates support variables like {language} which is filled in automatically. You can also define category tags that are suggested when editing photos.

Changing the active template and re-running AI analysis will regenerate descriptions for all affected photos.
prompts.examples: Example: create a template 'Describe this photo as a professional archivist would, noting date cues, attire, and setting' and assign it to your family history folder. Re-run analysis — all descriptions become more archivally detailed.

settings.title: Settings
settings.body:
The Settings page lets you change the default language for descriptions and the UI, set the default photo folder used when adding new photos, configure the backend API base URL (useful when running PhotoRAG server on a different machine), and toggle automatic processing when new photos are detected.

Language changes take effect immediately in the UI. If you change to a non-English language and descriptions have already been generated, click 'Re-translate all' to translate existing descriptions.
settings.examples: Example: change Default Language to Russian, click Save, then click 'Re-translate all'. All existing English descriptions are queued for translation. Future photos are automatically described and translated into Russian.

template-tags.title: Template Tags
template-tags.intro: Define the vocabulary of tags that the AI assigns to your photos.
template-tags.body:
Tags are short descriptive labels attached to photos — for example 'sunset', 'portrait', 'beach', or 'architecture'. The Template Tags page is where you manage the master list of tags that PhotoRAG recognises and can automatically assign during processing.

Each tag entry has two fields: a Name (the label shown in the UI and stored in the database) and a CLIP Prompt (a short natural-language phrase the CLIP visual model uses to detect whether this tag applies to a given photo). The CLIP prompt should describe what the tag looks like visually — for example the tag 'sunset' might have the CLIP prompt 'a photo taken at sunset with warm orange sky'.

When a photo is processed, the system runs every active CLIP prompt against the image and assigns tags whose visual similarity score exceeds the configured threshold. Tags are also suggested in the dropdown when you manually edit a photo.

You can create, edit, and delete tags here. Changes take effect for photos processed after the change; existing photos are not automatically re-tagged (re-run the scanner to update them).
template-tags.examples: Example: you want PhotoRAG to automatically tag all photos taken in winter. Create a tag with Name = 'winter' and CLIP Prompt = 'a snowy winter landscape with snow on the ground'. After saving, newly processed photos that visually match that description will receive the 'winter' tag automatically.

template-categories.title: Template Categories
template-categories.intro: Define the broader categories used to group your photos.
template-categories.body:
Categories are higher-level groupings than tags — for example 'Landscape', 'Portrait', 'Document', 'Event', or 'Architecture'. The Template Categories page works identically to Template Tags: each category has a Name and a CLIP Prompt that the visual model uses to detect whether a photo belongs to that category.

While a photo can have many tags, it is typically assigned to one primary category. Categories are used for high-level filtering in the Gallery and as a selection criterion in the AI Agent chat.

The intended workflow is: use Categories for broad grouping ('what kind of photo is this?') and Tags for specific content ('what specific subjects or themes are in this photo?'). Both appear as filter options in the Gallery and are included in semantic search indexing.

Create, edit, and delete categories here. Like tags, changes apply to future processing runs.
template-categories.examples: Example: create a category 'Document' with CLIP Prompt = 'a photo of a written or printed document, receipt, invoice, or form'. All newly processed photos of documents will be placed in the Document category, making it easy to filter your library to just document scans in the Gallery.
